units.title: Simple, compound and complex sentences
units.summary: The mix of sentence types examiners look for at band 6 and 7.

cards.title: Three types
cards.body:
- **Simple:** one clause. *Tourism creates jobs.*
- **Compound:** two main clauses joined by *and, but, so, or*. *Tourism creates jobs, but it can damage the environment.*
- **Complex:** a main clause + a subordinate clause (*because, although, which, if, when*). *Although tourism creates jobs, it can damage the environment.*
examples: If governments invest in transport, traffic will fall.
Cities, which are already crowded, will grow further.

cards.title: What examiners want
cards.body: Band 6: *a mix of simple and complex sentences*. Band 7: *a variety of complex structures* with *frequent error-free sentences*. Accuracy matters as much as range — three correct complex sentences beat ten with errors.

items: Because people are busy. They buy fast food.
Because people are busy, they buy fast food.
A 'because' clause alone is a fragment.
Although it is cheap, but it is unhealthy.
Although it is cheap, it is unhealthy.
Don't use although and but together.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Aim for at least one complex sentence in every body paragraph — often to explain a reason or a condition.
examples: While online learning is convenient, it requires a high level of self-discipline, which many students lack.

practice.q: Which is a complex sentence?
Although the city is crowded, [but] many people want to live there.
Which is correct?
o: Because it was raining. We stayed in.
Because it was raining, we stayed in.
Because it was raining we, stayed in.
practice.a: Because it was raining, we stayed in.

practice.q: Join with 'although': 'Cars are convenient. They cause pollution.'
practice.a: Although cars are convenient, they cause pollution.

practice.q: Join with 'which': 'The new law reduced crime. It was introduced in 2015.'
practice.a: The new law, which was introduced in 2015, reduced crime.

practice.q: Choose the best linker: 'Many students work part-time ___ they can pay their fees.'

units.title: Fragments, run-ons and comma splices
units.summary: The sentence-boundary errors that cap many essays at band 6.

cards.title: Fragment
cards.body: A group of words without a main clause.
examples: ✗ For example, the rise of online shopping.
✓ One example is the rise of online shopping.

cards.title: Comma splice
cards.body: Two complete sentences joined only by a comma. Fix with a full stop, a semicolon, or a conjunction.
examples: ✗ Technology is useful, it saves time.
✓ Technology is useful; it saves time.
✓ Technology is useful because it saves time.

cards.title: however is not a conjunction
cards.body: **However, therefore, moreover** connect sentences, not clauses. Use a full stop or semicolon before them.
examples: ✗ Cars are fast, however they pollute.
✓ Cars are fast. However, they pollute.
✓ Cars are fast; however, they pollute.

items: Many people live alone, this causes loneliness.
Many people live alone, and this causes loneliness.
Vehicles such as cars and buses are common.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Punctuation is part of Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Comma splices are one of the most common reasons strong essays stay at band 6.
examples: Public transport is cheap; however, it is often overcrowded.

practice.q: Which is correctly punctuated?
o: Exercise is important, it reduces stress.
Exercise is important because it reduces stress.
Exercise is important, because, it reduces stress.
practice.a: Exercise is important because it reduces stress.

practice.q: Which is correct?
o: Rents are high, however wages are low.
Rents are high. However, wages are low.
Rents are high however, wages are low.
practice.a: Rents are high. However, wages are low.

practice.q: Which is a complete sentence?
o: For instance, the growth of cities.
For instance, cities have grown rapidly.
Such as the growth of cities.
practice.a: For instance, cities have grown rapidly.

practice.q: Fix: 'Many young people move to cities ___ there are more jobs there.'
Tap the word that should be followed by a semicolon or full stop (choose where the first sentence ends): 'Some people prefer cities others prefer the countryside.'
Put the words in order.
practice.a: Public transport is cheap; however, it is often crowded.

units.title: Linking: reason, result, purpose, time
units.summary: because, since, as, so, therefore, so that, in order to, when, while, once.

cards.title: Reason
cards.body: **because / since / as + clause**; **because of / due to / owing to + noun**.
examples: Because traffic is heavy, many people cycle.
Due to heavy traffic, many people cycle.

cards.title: Result
cards.body: **so** (clause), **therefore / as a result / consequently** (new sentence), **so … that**.
examples: Fuel is expensive, so people drive less.
Fuel is expensive. As a result, people drive less.

cards.title: Purpose
cards.body: **to / in order to / so as to + verb**; **so that + clause**.
examples: Many students work in order to pay their fees.
Cities should build cycle lanes so that people can travel safely.

items: Because traffic is heavy, … / Due to heavy traffic, …
to save money / in order to save money

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Cause-and-effect reasoning is at the heart of Task 2. Mix clause and noun patterns for range.
examples: Owing to the rising cost of living, many young adults continue to live with their parents.

practice.q: ___ the bad weather, the match was cancelled.
She studied hard ___ pass the exam.
Housing is expensive. ___, many people rent.
[Due to] prices are rising, people are saving more.
Governments should tax sugar so ___ people eat less of it.
Which sentence is correct?
o: People exercise in order to staying healthy.
People exercise in order to stay healthy.
practice.a: People exercise in order to stay healthy.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: Many students work part-time in order to pay their fees.

units.title: Contrast and concession: although, despite, whereas, however

cards.title: Clause or noun?
cards.body:
- **although / even though / though + clause**
- **despite / in spite of + noun or -ing**
- **despite the fact that + clause**
examples: Although it was expensive, the project succeeded.
Despite the cost, the project succeeded.
Despite being expensive, the project succeeded.

cards.title: Comparing two things
cards.body: **whereas / while** join two contrasting facts in one sentence; **however / on the other hand / in contrast** start a new sentence.
examples: Coal use fell, whereas solar power rose.
Coal use fell. In contrast, solar power rose.

items: Despite it was cold, we swam.
Although it was cold, we swam. / Despite the cold, we swam.
In spite of the fact it rained, …
In spite of the fact that it rained, …
Whereas, the figure for women fell.
The figure for women, however, fell.
Whereas joins two clauses in one sentence.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Discussion essays and Task 1 comparisons depend on accurate contrast language.
examples: While some argue that zoos protect endangered species, others believe that keeping animals in cages is cruel.

practice.q: ___ the heavy rain, the event went ahead.
___ it was raining heavily, the event went ahead.
Men preferred football, ___ women preferred tennis.
[Despite] the price is high, many people buy it.
In spite of [study] hard, he failed.
Which sentence is correct?
o: Even though cars are convenient, they cause pollution.
Even though cars are convenient, but they cause pollution.
Even cars are convenient, they cause pollution.
practice.a: Even though cars are convenient, they cause pollution.

practice.q: Join with 'whereas': 'Sales of tea rose. Sales of coffee fell.'
practice.a: Sales of tea rose, whereas sales of coffee fell.

units.title: Defining relative clauses
units.summary: who, which, that, whose, where — identifying which one you mean.

cards.title: Pronouns
cards.body: **who** (people), **which** (things), **that** (people or things, informal), **whose** (possession), **where** (places), **when** (times).
examples: People who exercise live longer.
The city where I grew up has changed.
Students whose parents read to them read more.

cards.title: Leaving out the pronoun
cards.body: You can omit **who/which/that** when it is the **object** of the clause.
examples: The book (that) I bought is excellent.
The book that changed my life… (subject — cannot omit)

items: The man who he called me…
The city where I live / that I live in…
Place → where, or keep the preposition.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Relative clauses are the easiest way to build accurate complex sentences.
examples: Children who spend hours online may have fewer face-to-face friendships.

practice.q: Students ___ study regularly usually do better.
This is the town ___ I was born.
I met a woman ___ son is a pilot.
Countries [which] people live longer spend more on health.
The teacher who [she] taught me retired.
Which sentence is correct?
o: Jobs who pay well are competitive.
Jobs that pay well are competitive.
practice.a: Jobs that pay well are competitive.

practice.q: Join: 'People live near parks. They are often healthier.'
practice.a: People who live near parks are often healthier.

units.title: Non-defining relative clauses
units.summary: Extra information between commas — and 'which' referring to a whole idea.

cards.title: Extra information
cards.body: Non-defining clauses add information about something already identified. They use **commas**, and **that** is not allowed.
examples: Dhaka, which is one of the world's most crowded cities, is growing fast.
My sister, who lives in Canada, is a doctor.

cards.title: which = the whole idea
cards.body: **, which** can refer to the whole previous clause.
examples: Many people now work from home, which reduces traffic.
Car use fell by 20%, which was the largest drop in the period.

items: Many shops closed which led to job losses.
Many shops closed, which led to job losses.
Comma before 'which' for the whole idea.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: ', which…' is one of the most efficient band 7 structures in both tasks.
examples: Coal use fell sharply after 2010, which can be explained by the growth of renewables.

practice.q: Sylhet, ___ is famous for tea, attracts many tourists.
Prices doubled, ___ made life difficult for many families.
My brother, [that] works in a bank, lives in Dhaka.
Which is punctuated correctly?
o: The Amazon which is the largest rainforest is shrinking.
The Amazon, which is the largest rainforest, is shrinking.
The Amazon, that is the largest rainforest, is shrinking.
practice.a: The Amazon, which is the largest rainforest, is shrinking.

practice.q: Join with ', which': 'Many factories closed. This caused unemployment.'
practice.a: Many factories closed, which caused unemployment.

units.title: Reduced relative and participle clauses
units.summary: Shorter, more academic clauses with -ing and past participles.

cards.title: Reduced relatives
cards.body: **who/which + active verb → -ing**; **who/which + passive → past participle**.
examples: Students who live on campus → Students living on campus
Products which are made in China → Products made in China

cards.title: Participle clauses for time and reason
cards.body: **Having + pp** = after; **-ing** = at the same time / because.
examples: Having finished the course, she found a job.
Realising the danger, the government acted quickly.

items: Walking home, I was caught in the rain.
The subject of both parts must be the same.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Participle clauses add range and concision in Task 1 and Task 2.
examples: The number of cars rose steadily, reaching a peak of 3 million in 2010.

practice.q: People ___ in cities often have long commutes.
Most of the energy ___ in the country comes from gas.
Sales rose sharply, ___ (reach) a peak in 2015.
Goods [sending] by sea are cheaper to transport.
Which sentence is correct?
o: Having finished the report, she went home.
Having finish the report, she went home.
Finished the report, she went home.
practice.a: Having finished the report, she went home.

practice.q: Shorten: 'Students who study abroad gain independence.'

units.title: Noun clauses: that, what, whether, how
units.summary: Clauses that act as subjects or objects: 'What matters is…'

cards.title: that-clauses
cards.body: After verbs of thinking and saying: **believe / argue / suggest / claim that…**; after adjectives: **it is clear / likely / important that…**
examples: Many experts argue that homework is unnecessary.
It is clear that action is needed.

cards.title: wh- and whether clauses
cards.body: Use statement word order inside the clause.
examples: It is unclear whether the policy will work.
What young people need is more guidance.
Nobody knows how the problem started.

items: I don't know what is the answer.
I don't know what the answer is.
It is not clear if will it work.
It is not clear whether it will work.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: 'What + clause + is…' and 'It is … that…' add range and emphasis in Task 2 and Part 3.
examples: What worries many parents is the amount of time children spend online.

practice.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I wonder why is the sky blue.
I wonder why the sky is blue.
I wonder why blue is the sky.
practice.a: I wonder why the sky is blue.

practice.q: It is uncertain ___ the economy will recover.
___ students need most is practice.
Nobody knows how much [does it cost].
Put the words in order.
practice.a: It is widely believed that exercise improves mood.

units.title: Reported speech and reporting verbs
units.summary: Reporting what others say, and verbs like argue, claim, suggest.

cards.title: Tense backshift
cards.body: After a past reporting verb, tenses usually move back: present → past, will → would, present perfect → past perfect.
examples: 'I am tired.' → She said she was tired.
'We will help.' → They said they would help.

items: He told me that… / He said that…

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Discussion essays report views with varied reporting verbs instead of 'say'.
examples: Opponents of the plan claim that it would be too expensive.

practice.q: She ___ me that she was leaving.
'I will call you.' → He said he ___ call me.
The doctor suggested [to rest] for a week.
Critics ___ that the policy is unfair.
Which is correct?
o: He told to me the truth.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: Some experts argue that homework is unnecessary.

units.title: Zero and first conditionals
units.summary: General truths and real future possibilities.

cards.title: Zero conditional
cards.body: **If + present, present** — things that are always true.
examples: If you heat ice, it melts.
If people don't sleep enough, they find it hard to concentrate.

cards.title: First conditional
cards.body: **If + present, will / may / can + verb** — realistic future results.
examples: If the government raises fuel taxes, people will drive less.
If we don't act now, the problem may become worse.

cards.title: unless, as long as, provided that
cards.body: **unless** = if … not.
examples: Traffic will get worse unless public transport improves.

items: If it will rain, we will stay home.
If it rains, we will stay home.
Unless you don't study, you will fail.
Unless you study, you will fail.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Solution essays and Part 3 answers about consequences rely on the first conditional.
examples: If cities invested more in cycle lanes, more people would cycle — and if they do, air quality will improve.

practice.q: If you ___ (mix) red and white, you get pink.
If the bus ___ (be) late again, I will complain.
If taxes rise, people ___ less.
If the government [will invest] in education, the economy will grow.
Unless we [don't] reduce emissions, temperatures will keep rising.
Which sentence is correct?
o: If you won't hurry, you'll be late.
Unless you hurry, you'll be late.
Unless you won't hurry, you'll be late.
practice.a: Unless you hurry, you'll be late.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: If people recycle more, there will be less waste.

units.title: Second and third conditionals
units.summary: Imaginary present situations and imaginary pasts.

cards.title: Second conditional
cards.body: **If + past simple, would / could / might + verb** — imaginary or unlikely situations now or in the future. Use **were** for all persons in formal style.
examples: If I were the prime minister, I would make public transport free.
If public transport were cheaper, more people would use it.

cards.title: Third conditional
cards.body: **If + past perfect, would have + past participle** — imaginary past.
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed.
If the warnings had been heeded, the disaster might have been avoided.

items: If I would have money, I would travel.
If I had money, I would travel.
If I had known, I would help.
If I had known, I would have helped.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: 'If I were…' and 'If governments were to…' answers are excellent for hypothetical Part 3 questions.
examples: If young people had more opportunities in rural areas, fewer of them would move to the city.

practice.q: If I ___ (have) more time, I would learn Japanese.
If she had left earlier, she ___ (catch) the train.
If I ___ you, I would apply for the scholarship.
If people [would eat] less meat, emissions would fall.
If the government had acted sooner, fewer people [would lose] their jobs.
Which sentence is correct?
o: If cars were banned, cities would be quieter.
If cars would be banned, cities would be quieter.
If cars are banned, cities would be quieter.
practice.a: If cars were banned, cities would be quieter.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: If I had known, I would have helped you.

units.title: Mixed conditionals and alternatives to if
units.summary: Past cause with present result, and provided that, otherwise, were to.

cards.title: Mixed conditionals
cards.body: Past condition → present result: **If + past perfect, would + verb**.
examples: If I had taken that job, I would be living in London now.
If cities had been planned better, traffic would not be so bad today.

cards.title: Alternatives
cards.body: **provided / providing that, as long as, on condition that, otherwise, were + to-infinitive, should** (formal).
examples: The plan will work provided that it is properly funded.
Were the government to raise taxes, people would protest.
We need to act now; otherwise, costs will rise.

items: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. (correct)
Provided that it will be funded…

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: These structures signal C1-level grammatical range.
examples: Were governments to invest in rural infrastructure, migration to cities would slow.

practice.q: If I had saved more money, I ___ (be) rich now.
The project will succeed ___ it receives enough funding.
We must leave now; ___, we'll miss the flight.
Were the price [rise], demand would fall.
Put the words in order.
practice.a: The plan will work provided that it is properly funded.

cards.title: wish / if only
cards.body: **wish + past simple** (present regret), **wish + past perfect** (past regret), **wish + would** (annoyance or desire for change).
examples: I wish I spoke French.
I wish I had studied abroad.
I wish people would stop dropping litter.

cards.title: It's time
cards.body: **It's (high) time + subject + past simple** = it should happen now.
examples: It's time governments took climate change seriously.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Part 2 'explain how you felt' prompts invite wish and if only.
examples: Looking back, I wish I had taken more photos on that trip.

practice.q: I wish I ___ more free time.
I wish I ___ (listen) to my teacher's advice last year.
It's high time we [take] action on pollution.
Which is correct?
o: If only I knew the answer!
If only I know the answer!
If only I would know the answer!
practice.a: If only I knew the answer!

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: I wish I had started learning English earlier.
